claims.source: SP600125, a JNK inhibitor, suppressed ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization by LP (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 2), indicating that JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, as shown by no ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization 0.5 hr after LPS treatment despite strong JNK activation (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—source data 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by DSS crosslinking and immunoblotting data showing SP600125 reduced ASC oligomers (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.
claims.source: SP600125, a JNK inhibitor, suppressed ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization by LP (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 2), indicating that JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, as shown by no ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization 0.5 hr after LPS treatment despite strong JNK activation (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—source data 2).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that JNK inhibitor blocked ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, and that JNK activation alone (at 0.5 hr after LPS) did not induce ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.

claims.claim: IL-1β release by LP was inhibited by JNK inhibitor.
claims.source: Consistent with the roles of JNK in inflammasome activation by LP, IL-1β release by LP was inhibited by JNK inhibitor (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing SP600125 reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: IL-1β release by LP was not inhibited by 5Z-7-oxozeaenol, a TAK1 inhibitor.
claims.source: When we studied the roles of TAK1 as JNK upstream (Okada et al., 2014), IL-1β release by LP was not inhibited by 5Z-7-oxozeaenol, a TAK1 inhibitor (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1), in contrast to inflammasome activation by lysosomal rupture (Okada et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing no significant effect of 5Z-7-oxozeaenol on IL-1β release by LP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: IL-1β release by LP was significantly inhibited by selonsertib, an ASK1 inhibitor.
claims.source: IL-1β release by LP was significantly inhibited by selonsertib, an ASK1 inhibitor (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting the roles of ASK1 in inflammasome activation by LP.
claims.evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing selonsertib reduced IL-1β release by LP (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: ASK1 plays a role in inflammasome activation by LP.
claims.source: IL-1β release by LP was significantly inhibited by selonsertib, an ASK1 inhibitor (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting the roles of ASK1 in inflammasome activation by LP.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ASK1 inhibitor reduced inflammasome activation.

claims.claim: JNK activation by LP was inhibited by selonsertib.
claims.source: Consistently, JNK activation by LP was inhibited by selonsertib (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing selonsertib reduced JNK phosphorylation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).

claims.claim: ASK1 activation was observed at later time of LP treatment.
claims.source: Further, ASK1 activation was observed at later time of LP treatment (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2), suggesting that LP induces ASK1 activation likely through additional mechanisms such as lysosomal events at JNK upstream.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing ASK1 phosphorylation at later time points after LP treatment (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: LP induces ASK1 activation likely through additional mechanisms such as lysosomal events at JNK upstream.
claims.source: Further, ASK1 activation was observed at later time of LP treatment (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2), suggesting that LP induces ASK1 activation likely through additional mechanisms such as lysosomal events at JNK upstream.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ASK1 activation occurred at later time points, similar to delayed JNK activation.

claims.claim: ASK1 inhibitor blocked ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization as efficiently as JNK inhibitor.
claims.source: Consistent with the roles of ASK1 in JNK activation, ASK1 inhibitor blocked ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization as efficiently as JNK inhibitor (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), supporting that activated ASK1 induces JNK activation and subsequent ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.
claims.evidence: Supported by DSS crosslinking and immunoblotting data showing selonsertib reduced ASC oligomers (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: Activated ASK1 induces JNK activation and subsequent ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.
claims.source: Consistent with the roles of ASK1 in JNK activation, ASK1 inhibitor blocked ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization as efficiently as JNK inhibitor (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), supporting that activated ASK1 induces JNK activation and subsequent ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ASK1 inhibitor blocked both JNK activation and ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization.

claims.claim: ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor.
claims.source: When we studied the mechanism of ASK1 activation by LP, ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor, but not by KN-92, a KN-93 congener without CaMKII inhibitory activity (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), which supports the roles of increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII in ASK1 activation by LP, similar to the inhibition of lysosomal rupture-induced inflammasome by KN-93 (Okada et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-93 reduced ASK1 phosphorylation (Figure 7F).

claims.claim: ASK1 activation by LP was not attenuated by KN-92.
claims.source: When we studied the mechanism of ASK1 activation by LP, ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor, but not by KN-92, a KN-93 congener without CaMKII inhibitory activity (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), which supports the roles of increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII in ASK1 activation by LP, similar to the inhibition of lysosomal rupture-induced inflammasome by KN-93 (Okada et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-92 did not reduce ASK1 phosphorylation (Figure 7F).

claims.claim: Increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII play roles in ASK1 activation by LP.
claims.source: When we studied the mechanism of ASK1 activation by LP, ASK1 activation by LP was attenuated by KN-93, a CaMKII inhibitor, but not by KN-92, a KN-93 congener without CaMKII inhibitory activity (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), which supports the roles of increased [Ca2+]i and subsequent CAMKII in ASK1 activation by LP, similar to the inhibition of lysosomal rupture-induced inflammasome by KN-93 (Okada et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CaMKII inhibitor reduced ASK1 activation, and supported by citation to Okada et al., 2014.

claims.claim: JNK phosphorylation by LP was inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92.
claims.source: JNK phosphorylation and inflammasome activation as evidenced by maturation or release of IL-1β by LP were also inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92 (Figure 7F–H, Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduced JNK phosphorylation (Figure 7F).

claims.claim: IL-1β maturation by LP was inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92.
claims.source: JNK phosphorylation and inflammasome activation as evidenced by maturation or release of IL-1β by LP were also inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92 (Figure 7F–H, Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduced mature IL-1β (Figure 7G).

claims.claim: IL-1β release by LP was inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92.
claims.source: JNK phosphorylation and inflammasome activation as evidenced by maturation or release of IL-1β by LP were also inhibited by KN-93 but not by KN-92 (Figure 7F–H, Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduced IL-1β release (Figure 7H).

claims.claim: Increased [Ca2+]i due to lysosomal Ca2+ release facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization or NLRP3 inflammasome by LP and metabolic inflammation.
claims.source: These results indicate that increased [Ca2+]i due to lysosomal Ca2+ release facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization or NLRP3 inflammasome by LP and metabolic inflammation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the collective observations of lysosomal Ca2+ release, ER→lysosome refilling, K+ efflux through KCa3.1, CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway activation, and ASC oligomerization.

results.result: LPS + PA (LP) treatment induces lysosomal Ca2+ release in macrophages, evidenced by reduced perilysosomal Ca2+ release by GPN and decreased [Ca2+]Lys measurements, leading to increased cytosolic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C22, and C23 are well-supported by multiple complementary measurements including GCaMP3-ML1 imaging showing reduced GPN-induced perilysosomal Ca2+ release (Figure 1A), OGBD measurements showing decreased [Ca2+]Lys (Figure 1B), and Fluo-3-AM/Fura-2 measurements showing increased [Ca2+]i (Figure 1C). The inference that reduced GPN response indicates lysosomal Ca2+ depletion is reasonable and supported by citations to similar findings.

results.result: BAPTA-AM, a Ca2+ chelator, abrogates IL-1β release and maturation by LP without affecting pro-IL-1β levels, demonstrating that increased [Ca2+]i is functionally required for inflammasome activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by ELISA data showing BAPTA-AM reduces IL-1β release (Figure 1D) and immunoblotting showing reduced mature IL-1β without affecting pro-IL-1β levels (Figure 1E). The inference that BAPTA-AM's effect is unrelated to transcription/translation inhibition is reasonable given unchanged pro-IL-1β levels.

results.result: LP induces synergistic ROS accumulation, particularly mitochondrial ROS, which is functionally required for inflammasome activation and [Ca2+]i increase, as demonstrated by NAC and MitoTEMPOL inhibition experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C36 are well-supported by CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence showing LP induces more ROS than PA or LPS alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), MitoSOX data showing mitochondrial ROS accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and functional data showing NAC and MitoTEMPOL reduce both [Ca2+]i and IL-1β release (Figures 1E, 1F, 1—figure supplement 1B, 1—figure supplement 1C). The synergistic effect inference is reasonable.

results.result: TRPM2 is expressed on lysosomes of BMDMs and participates in LP-induced inflammasome through ADPR-mediated activation, as demonstrated by colocalization studies and inhibition by CD38 inhibitors (apigenin, quercetin).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by immunofluorescence showing TRPM2-LAMP2 colocalization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), ELISA data showing apigenin/quercetin reduce IL-1β release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and Ca2+ imaging showing these inhibitors reduce [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). The mechanism involving ADPR is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

results.result: Trpm2 knockout abrogates LP-induced [Ca2+]i increase, [Ca2+]Lys decrease, and inflammasome activation without affecting ROS production, indicating TRPM2 acts downstream of ROS in lysosomal Ca2+ release.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C52 are well-supported by comprehensive data showing Trpm2-KO prevents [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 2A), [Ca2+]Lys decrease (Figure 2B), IL-1β release (Figure 2C), and ASC speck formation (Figure 2D), while not affecting ROS production (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). The inference that TRPM2 is downstream of ROS is logical.

results.result: Trpm2 knockout inhibits inflammasome activation by lysosomotropic agents (LLOMe, MSU) but not by nigericin or ATP, indicating TRPM2 is specifically crucial for inflammasome involving lysosomal Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by ELISA data showing differential effects of Trpm2 KO on different inflammasome activators (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). The selectivity for lysosomotropic agents versus plasma membrane-acting agents (nigericin, ATP) provides strong evidence for lysosomal TRPM2 specificity.

results.result: Trpm2 knockout ameliorates HFD-induced metabolic inflammation and glucose intolerance in mice, with reduced blood glucose, improved IPGTT, reduced HOMA-IR, and decreased inflammasome markers (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage, CLS) in adipose tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C67 are comprehensively supported by in vivo data including blood glucose measurements (Figure 3A), IPGTT with AUC (Figure 3B), HOMA-IR calculations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), histological analysis of CLS (Figure 3C), ASC speck quantification (Figure 3D), and caspase-1 cleavage (Figure 3E). Body weight was controlled (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

results.result: LP does not activate plasma membrane TRPM2 current, as shown by patch clamp studies with ACA and cyclic ADPR, and bafilomycin A1 experiments demonstrate that lysosomal TRPM2 is the primary mediator of LP-induced [Ca2+]i increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C76 are supported by whole-cell patch clamp data showing LP does not affect plasma membrane TRPM2 current amplitude or basal activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), and bafilomycin A1 experiments showing that lysosomal Ca2+ depletion prevents TRPM2-dependent [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). This provides strong evidence for lysosomal versus plasma membrane TRPM2.

results.result: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs after LP-induced lysosomal Ca2+ release, as demonstrated by simultaneous monitoring showing [Ca2+]ER decrease paralleling [Ca2+]Lys recovery in Ca2+-free conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are well-supported by GEM-CEPIA1er and D1ER measurements showing [Ca2+]ER decrease after LP treatment in Ca2+-free medium (Figure 4A), and simultaneous monitoring showing inverse relationship between [Ca2+]ER and [Ca2+]Lys during recovery (Figure 4B). The temporal correlation provides strong evidence for ER→lysosome Ca2+ flux.

results.result: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs through IP3R channels (not RyR), as demonstrated by Xestospongin C and TPEN inhibition of [Ca2+]Lys recovery, and this refilling contributes functionally to inflammasome activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88 are supported by OGBD measurements showing Xestospongin C (IP3R inhibitor) and TPEN (ER Ca2+ chelator) prevent [Ca2+]Lys recovery while dantrolene (RyR inhibitor) does not (Figure 4C), and ELISA data showing Xestospongin C reduces IL-1β release (Figure 4D). The channel specificity and functional relevance are well-demonstrated.

results.result: LP induces ER-lysosome membrane contact sites, as shown by increased VAPA-ORP1L proximity ligation assay signals, which may facilitate ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by PLA data showing increased VAPA-ORP1L contacts after LP treatment (Figure 4E). The inference that these contacts facilitate Ca2+ refilling is reasonable and supported by citation to Yang et al., 2019, though the mechanistic link is not directly tested.

results.result: Store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE) is activated during LP-induced inflammasome to replenish ER Ca2+ stores, as demonstrated by EGTA, 2-APB, and BTP2 inhibition of inflammasome, and BTP2 reduction of [Ca2+]ER in LP-treated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 are well-supported by ELISA data showing EGTA, 2-APB, and BTP2 reduce IL-1β release (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, C), and D1ER measurements showing BTP2 reduces [Ca2+]ER in LP-treated cells when extracellular Ca2+ is present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). The functional role of SOCE is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: SOCE occurs through ORAI1 channels in LP-induced inflammasome, as evidenced by STIM1 aggregation and colocalization with ORAI1 after LP treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by confocal microscopy showing STIM1 puncta formation and colocalization with ORAI1 after LP treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E). These are established hallmarks of SOCE activation, and the inference is well-supported by citation to Vaca, 2010.

results.result: K+ efflux is coupled to SOCE in LP-induced inflammasome, as demonstrated by high extracellular K+ inhibiting inflammasome, reducing [Ca2+]ER, impairing [Ca2+]Lys recovery, and suppressing [Ca2+]i increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C109 are comprehensively supported by Potassium Green-2-AM showing [K+]i decrease (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), ELISA showing high [K+]e inhibits inflammasome (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), D1ER showing high [K+]e reduces [Ca2+]ER (Figure 5A), OGBD showing impaired [Ca2+]Lys recovery (Figure 5B), and Fluo-3-AM showing suppressed [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 5C). The coupling is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Ca2+-activated K+ channels, specifically KCa3.1 (not BK or SK channels, and not other K+ channels), mediate K+ efflux in LP-induced inflammasome, as shown by selective inhibitor studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C119 are well-supported by systematic pharmacological profiling showing charybdotoxin (pan-Ca2+-activated K+ channel inhibitor) and TRAM-34 (specific KCa3.1 inhibitor) reduce IL-1β release, while inhibitors of BK, SK, and other K+ channels do not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D). The selectivity for KCa3.1 is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: KCa3.1 channel facilitates Ca2+ influx after ER Ca2+ emptying and mediates K+ efflux during inflammasome, as shown by TRAM-34 revealing [Ca2+]ER decrease, inhibiting [Ca2+]i increase, and preventing [K+]i decrease.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 are supported by D1ER measurements showing TRAM-34 reveals [Ca2+]ER depletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), Fluo-3-AM/Fura-2 showing TRAM-34 reduces [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 5D), and Potassium Green-2-AM showing TRAM-34 prevents [K+]i decrease (Figure 5E). The positive role of KCa3.1 in Ca2+ influx is well-demonstrated.

results.result: BTP2 (SOCE inhibitor) suppresses both [Ca2+]i increase and [K+]i decrease by LP, likely by preventing Ca2+ influx that would activate KCa3.1 channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by Fluo-3-AM/Fura-2 and Potassium Green-2-AM measurements showing BTP2 prevents both Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux (Figure 5D, E). The inference that SOCE inhibition prevents KCa3.1 activation is logical and consistent with Ca2+-activated channel biology.

results.result: LP increases KCa3.1 channel activity without increasing Kcnn4 expression, as demonstrated by nystatin-perforated patch clamp showing increased TRAM-34-sensitive current and RT-PCR showing unchanged Kcnn4 mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133 are well-supported by nystatin-perforated patch clamp data showing increased TRAM-34-sensitive slope conductance after LP treatment (Figure 6A, B), RT-PCR showing no change in Kcnn4 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and validation in Kcnn4-KO cells showing no TRAM-34-sensitive current (Figure 6C, D). The technique validation strengthens the findings.

results.result: Kcnn4 knockout significantly reduces IL-1β release and inflammasome activation by LP, prevents [K+]i decrease, but does not affect TNF-α or IL-6 release, demonstrating KCa3.1 channel specificity for inflammasome.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C139 are supported by ELISA and immunoblotting showing reduced IL-1β release and caspase-1 cleavage in Kcnn4-KO cells (Figure 6E), Potassium Green-2-AM showing no [K+]i decrease (Figure 6F), and ELISA showing unchanged TNF-α/IL-6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). The specificity for inflammasome versus other inflammatory responses is well-demonstrated.

results.result: K+ efflux through KCa3.1 contributes to [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal, likely through facilitation of SOCE and subsequent ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling, as shown by TRAM-34 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are supported by OGBD measurements showing TRAM-34 prevents [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal (Figure 6G). The mechanistic inference linking K+ efflux to SOCE facilitation and ER→lysosome refilling is logical and consistent with the established coupling between these processes.

results.result: LP induces physical association between KCNN4 and ORAI1 channels in a Ca2+-dependent manner, which may facilitate functional coupling between K+ efflux and SOCE.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C145 are supported by PLA data showing increased KCNN4-ORAI1 contacts after LP treatment that are prevented by BAPTA-AM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D). However, the functional significance (claim C143) is speculative and only supported by citation, not direct experimental evidence. The Ca2+-dependence is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Kcnn4 knockout inhibits inflammasome by lysosomotropic agents (LLOMe, MSU) but not by nigericin or ATP, indicating KCa3.1 channel is specifically crucial for K+ efflux associated with lysosomal Ca2+ channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C150 are supported by ELISA data showing differential effects of Kcnn4 KO on different inflammasome activators (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E). The selectivity pattern mirrors that of Trpm2 KO, providing strong evidence for the lysosomal Ca2+-KCa3.1 axis specificity.

results.result: KCa3.1 channel is required for NLRP3 oligomerization and NLRP3-NEK7 binding in LP-induced inflammasome, as shown by Kcnn4 knockout or TRAM-34 treatment abrogating these interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C154 are supported by BN-PAGE showing reduced NLRP3 oligomers in Kcnn4-KO cells (Figure 6H) and immunoprecipitation showing reduced NLRP3-NEK7 binding with Kcnn4 KO or TRAM-34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, G). This links KCa3.1 to the core inflammasome assembly mechanism.

results.result: Kcnn4 knockout ameliorates HFD-induced metabolic inflammation in mice, with improved glucose tolerance and reduced inflammasome markers (caspase-1 cleavage, ASC specks, CLS) in adipose tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C158 are comprehensively supported by in vivo data including IPGTT showing improved glucose tolerance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), immunoblotting showing reduced caspase-1 cleavage (Figure 6I), immunofluorescence showing fewer ASC specks (Figure 6J), and histology showing fewer CLS (Figure 6K). This validates the in vitro findings in a disease-relevant model.

results.result: LP induces delayed JNK activation at 21 hr (distinct from early transient JNK activation by LPS alone at 30 min), suggesting different mechanisms depending on additional events such as lysosomal Ca2+ release.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C162 are supported by time-course immunoblotting showing biphasic JNK activation: early transient activation by LPS alone and delayed sustained activation by LP at 21 hr (Figure 7A). The inference of different mechanisms is reasonable given the distinct temporal patterns.

results.result: At 21 hr after LP treatment, [Ca2+]i, K+ efflux, and ER Ca2+ depletion are more pronounced than at 4 hr, suggesting full alteration of intracellular Ca2+ distribution occurs at later time points.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by time-course measurements showing higher [Ca2+]i (Fluo-3-AM), lower [K+]i (Potassium Green-2-AM), and reduced [Ca2+]ER (D1ER) at 21 hr compared to 4 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). This temporal progression is consistent with the delayed inflammasome activation.

results.result: ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization occur at 21 hr after LP treatment (but not at 0.5 hr after LPS alone despite similar JNK activation), indicating that delayed JNK activation with signal 2 (lysosomal events) is required.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C170 are supported by immunoblotting showing ASC phosphorylation (Figure 7B) and DSS crosslinking showing ASC oligomerization (Figure 7C) only at 21 hr after LP, not at 0.5 hr after LPS despite similar JNK activation levels. This demonstrates that JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient, requiring additional signals.

results.result: Delayed JNK activation by LP at 21 hr is suppressed by Kcnn4 or Trpm2 knockout, indicating that lysosomal Ca2+ release and/or K+ efflux are necessary for this delayed activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C173 are supported by immunoblotting showing reduced JNK phosphorylation in both Kcnn4-KO and Trpm2-KO cells treated with LP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). This links the lysosomal Ca2+-K+ efflux axis to delayed JNK activation.

results.result: JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization and inflammasome, as shown by SP600125 (JNK inhibitor) suppressing these events and the lack of ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization at 0.5 hr after LPS despite JNK activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C177 are supported by immunoblotting and DSS crosslinking showing SP600125 reduces ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), ELISA showing reduced IL-1β release (Figure 7E), and the temporal dissociation between JNK activation and ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization (Figures 7B, C). The necessity but insufficiency is well-demonstrated.

results.result: ASK1 (not TAK1) mediates delayed JNK activation in LP-induced inflammasome, as shown by selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) but not 5Z-7-oxozeaenol (TAK1 inhibitor) reducing IL-1β release and JNK activation, with ASK1 activation observed at later time points.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C183 are supported by ELISA showing selonsertib but not 5Z-7-oxozeaenol reduces IL-1β release (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), immunoblotting showing selonsertib reduces JNK phosphorylation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), and time-course showing ASK1 activation at later time points (Figure 7A). The pathway specificity is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Activated ASK1 induces JNK activation and subsequent ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, as shown by ASK1 inhibitor blocking these events as efficiently as JNK inhibitor.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C185 are supported by DSS crosslinking and immunoblotting showing selonsertib reduces ASC oligomerization and phosphorylation comparably to SP600125 (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). This establishes ASK1 as upstream of JNK in this pathway.

results.result: CaMKII mediates ASK1 activation by LP, as shown by KN-93 (CaMKII inhibitor) but not KN-92 (inactive analog) attenuating ASK1 activation, supporting roles of increased [Ca2+]i and CaMKII in ASK1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C188 are supported by immunoblotting showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduces ASK1 phosphorylation (Figure 7F). The use of the inactive analog KN-92 as a control strengthens the conclusion that CaMKII specifically mediates this effect. The mechanism is supported by citation to Okada et al., 2014.

results.result: CaMKII inhibition by KN-93 (but not KN-92) inhibits JNK phosphorylation, IL-1β maturation, and IL-1β release by LP, linking increased [Ca2+]i to inflammasome activation through the CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C191 are supported by immunoblotting showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduces JNK phosphorylation and mature IL-1β (Figures 7F, G), and ELISA showing reduced IL-1β release (Figure 7H). This completes the mechanistic pathway from Ca2+ to inflammasome activation.

results.result: The complete mechanistic pathway: increased [Ca2+]i due to lysosomal Ca2+ release (facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel) induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and metabolic inflammation.
results.evaluation: Claim C192 represents the integrated conclusion from all preceding results. It is well-supported by the comprehensive data showing: (1) lysosomal Ca2+ release through TRPM2, (2) ER→lysosome refilling through IP3R, (3) SOCE activation, (4) K+ efflux through KCa3.1 coupled to SOCE, (5) CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway activation, (6) ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, and (7) in vivo validation in HFD models. The mechanistic pathway is coherent and well-supported.

results.result: The authors claim that perilysosomal Ca2+ release by GPN was significantly reduced after LP treatment, suggesting lysosomal Ca2+ depletion by LP. This was measured using GCaMP3-ML1 transiently transfected into BMDMs (claims C22, C23).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 fundamentally challenges this foundational result, stating the approach is 'highly problematic' due to transient transfection of GCaMP3-ML1 into BMDMs. The reviewer notes that 'efficiency of transfection in BMDMs is always extremely low' and that 'overexpression results in gross mislocalization' with accumulation in the ER preventing credible measurements. The reviewer states 'the data are incredulous' and that 'these are foundational results, I cannot take the main claims of this study seriously.' Reviewer 3 also requests a positive control (e.g., ionomycin) to validate the GPN response, which was not provided.

results.result: The authors claim that LP decreased lysosomal Ca2+ and increased cytosolic Ca2+ through mitochondrial ROS, with functional roles demonstrated by BAPTA-AM abrogating IL-1β release and maturation without affecting pro-IL-1β levels (claims C1, C2, C24-C27).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 criticizes the cytosolic Ca2+ imaging approach, stating 'figure 1C doesn't make any sense. It looks like a snapshot of basal Ca2+ many hours after PA treatment - calcium elevations are highly dynamic. Snapshot measurements are not helpful.' The reviewer also notes that 'BAPTA-AM abrogates IL-1β secretion because IL-1β transcription is Ca2+ dependent - the result shown in figure 1D does not shed light on anything to do with inflammasome activation and it is misleading to suggest that.' This challenges the interpretation of the BAPTA-AM results. The lysosomal Ca2+ measurements using OGBD are not directly critiqued but rely on the problematic transfection approach.

results.result: The authors claim that TRPM2, expressed on lysosomes, mediates lysosomal Ca2+ release by LP, with evidence from Trpm2 KO experiments showing abrogation of Ca2+ changes and inflammasome activation, and pharmacological inhibition with apigenin/quercetin (claims C3, C37-C57).
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise multiple concerns about TRPM2 localization and function. Reviewer 1 states 'the study assumes that TRPM2 is a lysosomal ion channel. One paper reported TRPM2 in the lysosomes but this is a controversial claim, with no replication or further development in the last 14 years.' The reviewer notes that the localization data shown are 'problematic' with 'very high amounts of TRPM2 all across the cell - even more than LAMP2' and questions whether TRPM2 is being overexpressed. Reviewer 1 also criticizes the pharmacology: 'Apigenin and Quercetin are highly non-specific and their effects cannot be attributed to CD38 inhibition alone.' The patch clamp data are deemed 'very poor quality' with concerns about leak currents and missing Trpm2-/- controls. Reviewer 3 notes that 'the co-localization analyses failed to convincingly establish the lysosomal perimeter membrane residence of TRPM2' and that the suggested KO control for cADPR-induced currents was not performed.

results.result: The authors claim that Trpm2 KO ameliorated inflammasome activation and metabolic inflammation in HFD-fed mice, with improved glucose tolerance, reduced HOMA-IR, fewer crown-like structures, and reduced ASC specks and caspase-1 cleavage in adipose tissue (claims C4, C58-C67).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 challenges the interpretation of the in vivo metabolic phenotype, stating 'TRPM2 is expressed in many different cell lines. The broad metabolic differences observed by the authors in the Trpm2-/- mice cannot be attributed to macrophage-mediated inflammation. Such a conclusion requires the study of mice wherein Trpm2 is deleted selectively in macrophages or at least in the cells of the myeloid lineage.' This indicates that while the phenotypic data may be accepted, the mechanistic attribution to macrophage inflammasome activation is uncertain without cell-type-specific deletion.

results.result: The authors claim that ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs after lysosomal Ca2+ release through IP3R channels, with evidence from simultaneous monitoring of ER and lysosomal Ca2+, inhibition by Xestospongin C, and increased ER-lysosome contacts (claims C5, C6, C77-C90).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 fundamentally rejects this result, stating 'The ER-Lysosome Ca2+ refilling experiments rely on transient transfection of organelle-targeted sensors into BMDMs. See point #1 to understand why I find this approach to be highly problematic. Furthermore the data procured are also not convincing and lack critical controls (localization of sensors has not been demonstrated and their response to acute mobilization of Ca2+ has not been shown inspire any confidence in these results).' The reviewer's point #1 refers to the low transfection efficiency and mislocalization issues with transiently transfected sensors in BMDMs.

results.result: The authors claim that SOCE is activated following ER Ca2+ depletion, with evidence from STIM1 aggregation and colocalization with ORAI1, and inhibition of inflammasome by SOCE inhibitors BTP2 and 2-APB (claims C7, C8, C91-C101).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'there is no credible evidence that SOCE is activated in PA stimulated macrophages. The data shown in Fig 4 supp 1 do not investigate SOCE in a reliable manner - the conclusion is again based on snapshot measurements and crude non-selective inhibitors. The correct way to evaluate SOCE is to record cytosolic Ca2+ elevations over a period of time in absence and presence of extracellular Ca2+. However, even such recordings can be unreliable since the phenomenon is being investigated hours after PA stimulation. So, the only definitive way to demonstrate that Orai channels are indeed active during this process is through patch clamp electrophysiology of PA stimulated cells.' Reviewer 3 notes that the suggested experiment using YM-58483 (a SOCE inhibitor) was not performed.

results.result: The authors claim that SOCE is coupled with K+ efflux, with evidence that inhibiting K+ efflux (high extracellular K+) reduced ER Ca2+ content, impaired lysosomal Ca2+ recovery, and suppressed cytosolic Ca2+ increase (claims C9-C11, C102-C109).
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly critique the K+ efflux coupling experiments, the underlying SOCE activation evidence is challenged (see previous result). The coupling claim depends on the validity of SOCE activation, which Reviewer 1 states is not credibly demonstrated. The K+ measurements themselves are not specifically questioned, but the mechanistic interpretation linking them to SOCE is uncertain given the SOCE concerns.

results.result: The authors claim that LP activated KCa3.1 channel, a Ca2+-activated K+ channel, with evidence from nystatin-perforated patch clamp showing increased TRAM-34-sensitive K+ current, and that KCa3.1 contributes to Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux during inflammasome activation (claims C12, C110-C133).
results.evaluation: The KCa3.1 channel data using nystatin-perforated patch clamp and TRAM-34 are not directly criticized by reviewers. The pharmacological specificity with TRAM-34 and the validation using Kcnn4 KO cells (showing no TRAM-34-sensitive current) provide strong support. Reviewers do not raise concerns about these electrophysiological measurements or the KCa3.1 identification, in contrast to their critiques of the TRPM2 and SOCE data.

results.result: The authors claim that inhibitors of KCa3.1 channel or Kcnn4 KO reduced ER Ca2+, attenuated cytosolic Ca2+ increase and inflammasome activation by LP, with evidence showing effects on K+ efflux, lysosomal Ca2+ recovery, NLRP3 oligomerization, and NLRP3-NEK7 binding (claims C13-C17, C134-C154).
results.evaluation: The Kcnn4 KO and TRAM-34 inhibitor data are not directly challenged by reviewers. The genetic validation with Kcnn4 KO showing reduced inflammasome activation, K+ efflux, and effects on NLRP3 oligomerization provides strong support. The specificity of effects (e.g., inhibiting lysosomotropic agent-induced but not nigericin/ATP-induced inflammasome) strengthens the conclusions. Reviewers do not raise concerns about these results.

results.result: The authors claim that Kcnn4 KO ameliorated HFD-induced inflammasome and metabolic inflammation, with improved glucose tolerance, reduced caspase-1 cleavage, fewer ASC specks, and fewer crown-like structures in adipose tissue (claims C18, C19, C155-C158).
results.evaluation: The in vivo Kcnn4 KO metabolic phenotype data are not directly criticized by reviewers. Unlike the Trpm2 KO in vivo data, reviewers do not raise concerns about cell-type specificity for the Kcnn4 results. The phenotypic improvements in glucose tolerance and reduced inflammation markers in adipose tissue appear to be accepted.

results.result: The authors claim that lysosomal Ca2+ release induced delayed JNK and ASC phosphorylation through CaMKII-ASK1 pathway, with evidence showing JNK activation at 21 hr (but not 0.5 hr after LPS alone), ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization at 21 hr, and inhibition by KN-93 (CaMKII inhibitor) and selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) (claims C20, C21, C159-C191).
results.evaluation: The delayed JNK activation and CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway data are not directly criticized by reviewers. The temporal distinction between early JNK activation by LPS alone (0.5 hr) and delayed activation by LP (21 hr), along with the differential effects on ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, provide mechanistic insight. The pharmacological validation with specific inhibitors (KN-93 vs KN-92, selonsertib vs TAK1 inhibitor) and genetic validation (Kcnn4 KO, Trpm2 KO) support the pathway. Reviewers do not raise concerns about these signaling results.

results.result: The authors claim that LP induced ROS accumulation (synergistic effect of LPS and PA), particularly mitochondrial ROS, which was reduced by NAC and MitoTEMPOL, with functional roles in Ca2+ increase and inflammasome activation (claims C28-C36).
results.evaluation: The ROS data using CM-H2DCFDA and MitoSOX are not directly criticized by reviewers. The demonstration of synergistic ROS production by LP compared to LPS or PA alone, and the functional validation with antioxidants (NAC, MitoTEMPOL) reducing both Ca2+ increase and inflammasome activation, appear to be accepted. These are supporting mechanistic data rather than foundational claims.

results.result: The authors claim that LP does not affect plasma membrane TRPM2 current based on patch clamp experiments with cyclic ADPR, and that bafilomycin A1 abrogated TRPM2-dependent Ca2+ increase, supporting lysosomal TRPM2 involvement (claims C68-C76).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the patch clamp data are 'of very poor quality' and questions whether the results represent 'leak currents seen in measurements with substandard seals.' The reviewer notes 'Even with such high concentrations of cADPr, the TRPM2 current is tiny and Trpm2-/- controls are missing. The current-voltage relationship is not shown.' The reviewer also states '20 uM ACA is not a selective inhibitor of TRPM2 - relying on ACA as the conclusive diagnostic is problematic.' These technical concerns undermine the conclusions about plasma membrane vs lysosomal TRPM2.

results.result: The authors present an integrated model claiming that increased cytosolic Ca2+ due to lysosomal Ca2+ release facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization and NLRP3 inflammasome activation (claim C192).
results.evaluation: This overarching model integrates multiple results, some of which are unsupported or uncertain. While the KCa3.1 and CaMKII-ASK1-JNK components are supported, the foundational lysosomal Ca2+ release measurements, TRPM2 localization/function, ER→lysosome refilling, and SOCE activation are all challenged by reviewers. The editor's summary states 'the major claims of the article are thus only incompletely supported,' and Reviewer 1 concludes 'this is very poor-quality science.' The model's validity depends on the problematic foundational Ca2+ dynamics data.

comparisons.comparison: Both address lysosomal Ca2+ measurements using GCaMP3-ML1 (C22, C23). OpenEval finds the data well-supported by multiple complementary measurements. Peer reviewers fundamentally reject this result as 'highly problematic' due to transient transfection issues in BMDMs, stating 'efficiency of transfection in BMDMs is always extremely low' and 'overexpression results in gross mislocalization' preventing credible measurements.

OpenEval R1 addresses cytosolic Ca2+ measurements (C1, C2) as part of comprehensive support for lysosomal Ca2+ depletion. Peer R2 challenges these cytosolic Ca2+ measurements (C1, C2), stating 'figure 1C doesn't make any sense' and that 'snapshot measurements are not helpful' for dynamic Ca2+ elevations.

Both evaluate BAPTA-AM effects on IL-1β release (C24-C27). OpenEval finds the data support that BAPTA-AM's effect is unrelated to transcription/translation inhibition. Peer reviewers challenge this interpretation, stating 'BAPTA-AM abrogates IL-1β secretion because IL-1β transcription is Ca2+ dependent' and that the result 'is misleading to suggest that' it relates to inflammasome activation.

Both address ROS production claims (C28-C36). OpenEval finds the data well-supported by CM-H2DCFDA and MitoSOX measurements showing synergistic ROS production and functional validation with antioxidants. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these ROS data, appearing to accept them as supporting mechanistic evidence.

Both evaluate TRPM2 localization and function (C37-C44). OpenEval finds the colocalization and pharmacological data supportive. Peer reviewers raise fundamental concerns: 'TRPM2 is a lysosomal ion channel' is 'a controversial claim, with no replication,' localization data show 'very high amounts of TRPM2 all across the cell,' and 'Apigenin and Quercetin are highly non-specific.'

Both address TRPM2 knockout effects on Ca2+ dynamics and inflammasome (C45-C52). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from multiple measurements. Peer reviewers question the underlying TRPM2 localization and function claims, with concerns about whether TRPM2 is truly lysosomal and whether the data quality supports the conclusions.

Both evaluate TRPM2 selectivity for different inflammasome activators (C53-C57). OpenEval finds the differential effects provide strong evidence for lysosomal TRPM2 specificity. Peer reviewers' concerns about TRPM2 localization and function (from R3) extend to questioning the interpretation of these selectivity data.

Both address in vivo metabolic phenotype of Trpm2 KO mice (C58-C67). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from glucose measurements, IPGTT, histology, and inflammasome markers. Peer reviewers challenge the mechanistic attribution, stating 'The broad metabolic differences observed...cannot be attributed to macrophage-mediated inflammation' without cell-type-specific deletion.

Both evaluate plasma membrane vs lysosomal TRPM2 using patch clamp (C68-C76). OpenEval finds the data provide strong evidence for lysosomal versus plasma membrane TRPM2. Peer reviewers reject this, stating the patch clamp data are 'of very poor quality,' questioning whether results represent 'leak currents,' noting 'Trpm2-/- controls are missing,' and that '20 uM ACA is not a selective inhibitor.'

Both address ER→lysosome Ca2+ flux (C77-C81). OpenEval finds strong support from GEM-CEPIA1er and D1ER measurements showing temporal correlation. Peer reviewers fundamentally reject this, stating 'ER-Lysosome Ca2+ refilling experiments rely on transient transfection' which is 'highly problematic,' and 'the data procured are also not convincing and lack critical controls.'

Both evaluate IP3R involvement in ER→lysosome Ca2+ transfer (C82-C88). OpenEval finds support from Xestospongin C and TPEN effects. Peer reviewers reject the underlying ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling data due to transfection issues and lack of controls, undermining these mechanistic claims.

Both address VAPA-ORP1L contacts facilitating Ca2+ refilling (C89-C90). OpenEval finds PLA data supportive though mechanistic link not directly tested. Peer reviewers' rejection of the ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling approach extends to questioning these contact site data.

Both evaluate SOCE activation and its role in inflammasome (C91-C98). OpenEval finds support from pharmacological inhibitors and D1ER measurements. Peer reviewers state 'there is no credible evidence that SOCE is activated,' criticizing 'snapshot measurements and crude non-selective inhibitors,' and stating 'the only definitive way' is patch clamp electrophysiology.

Both address STIM1-ORAI1 colocalization as evidence of SOCE (C99-C101). OpenEval finds confocal microscopy data supportive. Peer reviewers' rejection of SOCE activation evidence extends to questioning whether these colocalization data demonstrate functional SOCE in this context.

Both evaluate K+ efflux coupling to SOCE and ER Ca2+ (C102-C109). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from multiple measurements. Peer reviewers note that while K+ measurements themselves aren't questioned, the mechanistic interpretation linking them to SOCE is uncertain given the challenged SOCE activation evidence.

Both address KCa3.1 channel identification and selectivity (C110-C119). OpenEval finds systematic pharmacological profiling supportive. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these data, and the pharmacological specificity with TRAM-34 and Kcnn4 KO validation appear accepted.

Both evaluate KCa3.1's positive role in Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux (C120-C125). OpenEval finds support from TRAM-34 effects on multiple Ca2+ and K+ measurements. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these KCa3.1 functional data.

Both address SOCE inhibition preventing KCa3.1 activation (C126-C128). OpenEval finds the inference logical based on BTP2 effects. Peer reviewers' concerns about SOCE evidence may extend to this coupling claim, though the KCa3.1 data themselves are not directly challenged.

Both evaluate nystatin-perforated patch clamp data showing KCa3.1 activation (C129-C133). OpenEval finds strong support including Kcnn4 KO validation. Peer reviewers do not critique these electrophysiological measurements, in contrast to their concerns about TRPM2 patch clamp data.

Both address Kcnn4 KO effects on inflammasome and K+ efflux (C134-C139). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from genetic validation. Peer reviewers do not challenge these Kcnn4 KO data, and the genetic approach with specificity for inflammasome appears accepted.

Both evaluate TRAM-34 preventing lysosomal Ca2+ recovery (C140-C141). OpenEval finds support linking K+ efflux to ER→lysosome refilling. Peer reviewers' rejection of the ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling measurements may extend to questioning this mechanistic link.

Both address KCNN4-ORAI1 contacts and their functional significance (C142-C145). OpenEval notes functional significance is speculative. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these PLA data, though the underlying SOCE concerns may affect interpretation.

Both evaluate Kcnn4 KO selectivity for different inflammasome activators (C146-C150). OpenEval finds the selectivity pattern provides strong evidence. Peer reviewers do not challenge these selectivity data for Kcnn4 KO.

Both address Kcnn4 KO effects on NLRP3 oligomerization and NEK7 binding (C151-C154). OpenEval finds support linking KCa3.1 to inflammasome assembly. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these mechanistic data.

Both evaluate in vivo Kcnn4 KO metabolic phenotype (C155-C158). OpenEval finds comprehensive support validating in vitro findings. Peer reviewers do not critique these in vivo Kcnn4 data, unlike their concerns about Trpm2 KO requiring cell-type-specific deletion.

Both address biphasic JNK activation with distinct temporal patterns (C159-C162). OpenEval finds support from time-course immunoblotting. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these JNK activation data.

Both evaluate temporal progression of Ca2+, K+, and ER Ca2+ changes (C163-C167). OpenEval finds time-course measurements supportive. Peer reviewers do not directly challenge these temporal data, though underlying Ca2+ measurement concerns may apply.

Both address JNK activation being necessary but insufficient for ASC phosphorylation (C168-C170). OpenEval finds temporal dissociation demonstrates this. Peer reviewers do not critique these ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization timing data.

Both evaluate Kcnn4 KO and Trpm2 KO effects on JNK phosphorylation (C171-C173). OpenEval finds support linking the Ca2+-K+ axis to JNK. Peer reviewers do not directly challenge these signaling connections.

Both address JNK inhibitor effects on ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization and IL-1β (C174-C177). OpenEval finds comprehensive support for JNK's role. Peer reviewers do not critique these pharmacological validation data.
Both evaluate ASK1-JNK pathway specificity using selonsertib (C178-C183). OpenEval finds strong support for pathway specificity. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these ASK1 inhibitor data.
Both address selonsertib effects on ASC oligomerization/phosphorylation (C184-C185). OpenEval finds support establishing ASK1 upstream of JNK. Peer reviewers do not challenge these data.

Both evaluate CaMKII mediating ASK1 phosphorylation using KN-93 vs KN-92 (C186-C188). OpenEval finds the inactive analog control strengthens conclusions. Peer reviewers do not critique these CaMKII data.
Both address CaMKII inhibitor effects on JNK and IL-1β (C189-C191). OpenEval finds support completing the mechanistic pathway. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these data.

Both evaluate the overarching integrated model (C192). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from all preceding results forming a coherent pathway. Peer reviewers conclude the model is only 'incompletely supported' because foundational lysosomal Ca2+ measurements, TRPM2 localization/function, ER→lysosome refilling, and SOCE activation are all challenged, despite KCa3.1 and CaMKII-ASK1-JNK components being supported.
